question: What is diluted EPS, and what was NVIDIA's in fiscal 2026?
answer:

question: Looking at AMD, what is the company's growth? What factors are responsible? Are those sustainable factors or just spikes?
answer:
AMD's revenue grew 34% in fiscal 2025 (year ended December 27, 2025), from $25.8 billion to $34.6 billion. That follows 14% growth in 2024. The filings show some lasting drivers and some that look more cyclical. They don't label any driver as permanent or a one-off.

## What the filing says
- **Overall growth:** Net revenue rose to $34.6B in 2025 from $25.8B in 2024 (+34%) [AMD FY2025 10-K, p.63]. 2024 was up from $22.7B in 2023, which I calculate as about +14% [AMD FY2024 10-K, p.62].
- **Data Center (the AI and server chips segment):** Revenue was $16.6B, up 32%. AMD credits demand for its EPYC server processors and Instinct MI350 AI GPUs (graphics chips used for AI) [AMD FY2025 10-K, p.63]. This followed a 94% jump in 2024 [AMD FY2024 10-K, p.60].
- **Client and Gaming (PC and console chips):** Revenue was $14.6B, up 51%. PC processor shipments rose 31% and average selling price rose 15%. Gaming rose 51% on higher semi-custom revenue (chips custom-built for customers, such as consoles) and Radeon GPU demand [AMD FY2025 10-K, pp.63, 68]. Gaming had fallen 58% in 2024 [AMD FY2024 10-K, p.60].
- **Embedded:** Revenue fell 3% to $3.5B because "certain end market demand remained mixed" [AMD FY2025 10-K, p.63]. It had fallen 33% in 2024 [AMD FY2024 10-K, p.54].
- **Caveats on durability:**
  - The filing calls the semiconductor industry "highly cyclical" and says AMD has "incurred substantial losses in previous downturns" [AMD FY2025 10-K, p.28].
  - It says the "near-term and long-term trajectory" of generative AI is unknown. Data center construction delays or customers' difficulty raising capital could delay demand [AMD FY2025 10-K, p.30].
  - U.S. export rules on MI308 chips for China caused about $800M of charges. About $360M was reversed once licenses came through, leaving about $440M net. Future China sales depend on licenses [AMD FY2025 10-K, pp.45, 68].

## What this might mean
This is my own reading. Data Center growth rests on AMD's AI and server product roadmap, which looks like a structural driver, but the filing says AI demand is uncertain. Client and Gaming grew faster than Data Center in 2025, and Gaming and Embedded have swung sharply in recent years. That pattern suggests parts of the growth are cyclical rather than steady.

question: Why did Apple's profit drop in 2024 even though sales went up?
answer:
Apple's net income (profit after all costs and taxes) fell in fiscal 2024, which ended Sept 28, 2024. It dropped from $97.0 billion to $93.7 billion even though net sales rose 2%. The cause was a one-time $10.2 billion income tax charge. Profit from running the business actually rose.

- **The main reason was a one-time charge.** Apple booked a $10.2 billion net charge tied to the European Commission's "State Aid Decision." The EC had ruled that Ireland gave Apple unlawful tax benefits, and Ireland was ordered to recover additional taxes from Apple. [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.28; p.42]
- **Two smaller tax factors.** The filing also cites a higher tax rate on foreign earnings and smaller tax benefits from employee stock compensation. [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.28]
- **The result:** net income was $93,736 million versus $96,995 million, a drop of about $3.3 billion (about 3.4%). [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.32]

question: What's the deal between Microsoft and OpenAI?
answer:
Microsoft's FY2026 10-K (year ended June 30, 2026) describes OpenAI as a long-term strategic partner that Microsoft invests in, earns revenue from and licenses technology from. Microsoft holds about a 25% stake, and the partnership was extended in October 2025 and April 2026.

## What the filing says
- **Ownership:** Microsoft has an equity-method investment (it records its share of the investee's profit or loss) of about 25% in OpenAI "on an as-converted basis." Its funding commitments total $13.0 billion, and $11.9 billion had been funded by June 30, 2026. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.60]
- **History and extensions:** The partnership started in 2019. A new definitive agreement was signed in October 2025, and it was extended again in April 2026. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.34, p.60]
- **Technology rights:** Microsoft holds rights to OpenAI's intellectual property, including models and infrastructure, to build into its own products. It "will continue to receive revenue-sharing payments." [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.34]
- **Money flowing in:** Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion of FY2026 revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing. OpenAI owed Microsoft $6.0 billion in receivables at year-end. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.60]
- **Ownership change:** OpenAI formed a public benefit corporation and recapitalized in October 2025. Microsoft's share fell as a result and from other funding, and Microsoft booked dilution gains. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.60]
- **Effect on profit:** OpenAI investment results added $5.0 billion to FY2026 net income. In FY2025 they cut net income by $3.6 billion. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.38]
- **Earlier terms (FY2025):** The OpenAI API was exclusive to Azure, and Microsoft had a right of first refusal on OpenAI's new capacity needs. I didn't find whether these still apply in the FY2026 filing. [Microsoft FY2025 10-K, p.35]

## What this might mean
This is my reading, not the company's. Microsoft is both an owner of OpenAI and a large commercial partner, so the relationship affects its income statement in two ways: revenue from OpenAI and swings in the value of its stake. Because those swings can move reported profit up or down, Microsoft's non-GAAP measures leave them out.

question: How does a bank like JPMorgan make money?
answer:
JPMorgan Chase earns money mainly from the gap between what it earns on loans and investments and what it pays on deposits and debt, and from fees and trading. In 2025 it reported $182.4 billion of total net revenue and $57.0 billion of net income. About 52% of the revenue was interest-related and about 48% was fees and similar income.

## What the filing says
- **Interest spread:** Net interest income (NII, interest earned minus interest paid) was $95.4 billion in 2025, up 3% [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.49]. Interest earned was about $193.8 billion and interest paid about $97.9 billion, on a taxable-equivalent basis (an adjustment for tax-exempt income) [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.317]. That is 95.4 ÷ 182.4 ≈ 52% of revenue.
- **Fees and other income:** Noninterest revenue was $87.0 billion, about 48% of revenue (87.0 ÷ 182.4) [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.49]. It includes investment banking fees ($9.6 billion), asset management fees, card income and deposit-related fees [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.220].
- **Trading ("Markets"):** Markets revenue was $35.8 billion, up 19% [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.49].
- **Four revenue sources:** On a managed basis (adjusted for tax-exempt income), revenue was $185.6 billion. Of that, Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) brought in $76.0 billion and the Commercial & Investment Bank (CIB) $78.5 billion [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, pp.68, 73]. Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) brought in $24.1 billion and Corporate $7.0 billion [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, pp.78, 83]. The four add up to about $185.6 billion.
- **From revenue to profit:** Expenses were $95.6 billion, leaving pre-provision profit of $86.8 billion. Setting aside $14.2 billion for expected loan losses gives about $72.6 billion before income taxes, and net income was $57.0 billion [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.49].

## What this might mean
This is my own reading. A bank is partly a spread business, borrowing cheaply and lending at higher rates. It is also partly a fee business, charging for advice, payments, trading and managing money. Roughly half of the revenue comes from each, and the money set aside for bad loans shows that lending carries risk.

question: How much did JPMorgan set aside for bad loans?
answer:
JPMorgan Chase set aside $14.2 billion as its provision for credit losses in fiscal 2025 (year ended December 31, 2025). That's up from $10.7 billion in 2024. The "provision for credit losses" is the amount a bank puts aside as an expense to cover loans that may not be repaid.

- The 2025 total provision was $14,212 million, against $10,678 million in 2024 and $9,320 million in 2023. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.55]
- It splits into $9.8 billion of net charge-offs (loans written off as uncollectable, minus later recoveries) and a $4.4 billion net addition to the allowance (the cushion held for future losses). $9.8B + $4.4B = $14.2B. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.55]
- Consumer lending was $11,522 million of the total, including $10,829 million for credit cards. Wholesale (loans to businesses and institutions) was $2,718 million. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.55]

- Wholesale provisions reflected loan growth, an update to loss assumptions on certain leveraged loans, and estimated losses from borrower fraud in certain secured lending facilities. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.55]
- The 2025 total is about 33% higher than 2024: ($14,212M − $10,678M) ÷ $10,678M. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.55]

## What this might mean
This is my reading, not the company's. Most of the money set aside went to credit cards, and the filing ties that to loan growth. The rise from 2024 came from both more actual write-offs and a bigger cushion for expected future losses, and part of that cushion was linked to a specific deal (Apple Card).

question: Is NVIDIA investing in AI companies that in turn are buying their chips/services? Is this also true for AMD?
answer:
**NVIDIA:** Yes, in part. In fiscal 2026 (year ended Jan 25, 2026), NVIDIA put $17.5 billion into private companies, and that included AI model makers that buy its products. **AMD:** It's a different arrangement. In 2025 (year ended Dec 27, 2025), AMD gave OpenAI the right to buy AMD shares under a GPU purchase deal. The filings don't show AMD investing cash in AI customers the way NVIDIA does.

## What the filing says
- NVIDIA "invested $17.5 billion in private companies and infrastructure funds, primarily to support early-stage startups." It says these "include AI model makers that purchase our products directly or through CSPs" (cloud service providers). [NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, p.37]

- NVIDIA warns that these startups may not become profitable and that it could lose all or part of the investments. [NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, p.22]
- AMD signed a product purchase agreement with OpenAI in October 2025 to deploy 6 gigawatts of AMD GPUs. At the same time, it issued OpenAI a warrant for up to 160 million AMD shares at $0.01 each. - None of the warrant shares had vested by Dec 27, 2025, and the warrant had no effect on AMD's financial statements that year. [AMD FY2025 10-K, p.103]

This is my reading. NVIDIA's filing openly says some of its investment money goes to companies that are also its customers. AMD's link to OpenAI works the other way.
